The Reserve

Ecology and restorative justice, growing from the same roots

In 2023, the Crecer en Paz Foundation gifted 400 hectares of tropical dry forest to Sembrandopaz, which now stewards the land as Morrocoy Nature Reserve. It sits in El Salado, El Carmen de Bolívar, a community still healing from years of conflict.

Today the reserve is dedicated to conserving and reforesting Tropical Dry Forest, one of the most endangered ecosystems on Earth, while giving the surrounding community a stake in what grows back.

The Land

One reserve, two plots

The 400 hectares of Morrocoy aren't one unbroken block — the reserve is made up of two adjoining plots, Morrocoy 1 and Morrocoy 2, mapped and monitored across El Salado, El Carmen de Bolívar.

Morrocoy 1 — southern plot
Morrocoy 2 — northern plot
// Morrocoy 1 & 2, mapped from our own survey
What restoration looks like

From open scar to closed canopy

Both plots were left exposed by mining activity before Sembrandopaz began reforesting them. This is the starting point every hectare of today's forest had to grow back from.

Reforesting land like this isn't instant — closed-canopy tropical dry forest takes years of active planting, monitoring, and protection to return. Every gift to Morrocoy funds that work.

Who lives here

Home to thousands of species, some found nowhere else

The reserve shelters endangered wildlife alongside San Pedrito, a 24-acre site built for eco-tourism and environmental education.

Cottontop Tamarin

One of the world's most endangered primates, native to this stretch of forest.

Keel-billed Toucan

A signature sighting for visitors exploring San Pedrito's trails.

Thousands of plant species

The backbone of a dry-forest ecosystem under active reforestation.

Programs

Teaching the next generation to protect what's theirs

Education is at the center of Morrocoy — not an add-on to conservation, but the reason it lasts.

School in the Forest

Classrooms with no walls

Children learn ecology, biology, and stewardship directly in the reserve — turning the forest itself into the curriculum.

Ecological Youth Protectors

Young people, leading

A youth program that builds leadership and care — for the forest, for themselves, and for their communities.

San Pedrito
Visit

Come see the forest for yourself

San Pedrito is the reserve's 24-acre eco-tourism and education site — trails, an environmental education center, and a base for the School in the Forest program, tucked into the tree line above El Salado.
